title: Bounded Rationality
description: Why real humans aren't homo economicus — Simon, satisficing, cognitive limits

concepts.title: Homo Economicus and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Standard economics rests on a stylized agent: homo economicus — perfectly rational, fully informed, computationally unlimited, maximizing expected utility over consistent preferences.

This was always known to be a fiction. The question is whether it's a useful fiction — a good approximation that yields the right comparative statics — or a misleading one that gets actual behavior wrong in important ways.

Behavioral economics emerged from the conviction that the deviations are systematic, predictable, and important enough to incorporate into economic models. Not random noise around perfect optimization, but real psychology with structure of its own.

concepts.title: Herbert Simon and Bounded Rationality
concepts.contentHtml:
Herbert Simon (Nobel 1978) coined bounded rationality: humans intend to be rational but are limited by cognitive capacity, time, and information.

Real decision-makers can't survey all options, can't compute optimal solutions, can't perfectly forecast consequences. Instead they use heuristics — shortcuts that work well enough most of the time.

Simon's critique wasn't that people are irrational. It was that 'fully rational' isn't a coherent benchmark for finite minds in complex environments. Better to study the actual decision processes — and how they cope, succeed, and fail.

concepts.title: Satisficing
concepts.contentHtml:
Simon's positive proposal: satisficing. Instead of maximizing utility, decision-makers set an aspiration level — a satisfactory threshold — and pick the first option that meets it.

Job hunters don't survey every possible firm before deciding; they take the first acceptable offer. Apartment hunters don't tour every flat in town. Shoppers don't compare every grocery option.

Satisficing isn't always suboptimal. Search has costs; full optimization may be infeasible or pointless. The aspiration level itself adapts — too easy and it rises, too hard and it falls. The result is bounded but functional choice.

Many algorithms in computer science work the same way: greedy heuristics, local search, anytime algorithms. They don't guarantee optimum but reliably produce 'good enough' in tractable time.

concepts.title: Two Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
Daniel Kahneman's framework popularized the dual-process view: humans use two cognitive systems.

System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive, parallel, effortless. It handles most of life — recognizing faces, driving familiar routes, gut reactions.

System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytical, serial, effortful. It handles unfamiliar problems, calculations, weighing options.

Many of the systematic biases studied in behavioral economics arise when System 1 produces a quick answer and System 2 doesn't override it — either because we're tired, distracted, time-pressed, or because the System 1 answer feels obviously right.

The dual-process model isn't precise neuroscience, but it's a useful organizing metaphor for the difference between automatic and controlled cognition.

concepts.title: Why Bounded Rationality Matters for Economics
concepts.contentHtml:
If people are boundedly rational, several economic predictions change.

Search frictions become endogenous, not just exogenous costs. Information matters more — the same options framed differently produce different choices. Default options have outsize influence (because nobody re-optimizes from scratch). Education and decision aids can have real effects on welfare.

Markets correct some of this — repeated experience, professional intermediaries, competition — but not all. Especially in one-shot, high-stakes, complex decisions (mortgages, retirement saving, healthcare plans), boundaries on rationality aren't sanded away by market forces.

This opens the door for behavioral policy: design choice architectures that work with — not against — actual human cognition.

title: Prospect Theory
description: Kahneman and Tversky — loss aversion, reference dependence, S-shaped value

concepts.title: What Expected Utility Misses
concepts.contentHtml:
The standard model of risky choice is expected utility theory: rank gambles by E[u(W)], where u is a concave utility function over final wealth W.

Kahneman and Tversky's experiments uncovered systematic violations.

People prefer a sure $500 to a 50-50 gamble of $0 or $1100, even though the expected value is $550 — risk aversion, fine. But they also prefer a 50-50 gamble of $0 or –$1100 to a sure loss of $500. Risk-loving in losses, risk-averse in gains. EU theory can't accommodate both with a single utility function over wealth.

Their prospect theory (1979) replaces EU with a model that fits the actual patterns.

concepts.title: Reference Dependence
concepts.contentHtml:
The first key change: people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, not as final wealth levels.

The reference point is usually the status quo — but it can be expectations, recent peaks, an aspiration. A trader anchored to last week's high feels a loss even when sitting on profits.

Reference dependence implies that identical economic outcomes feel different depending on the comparison. A $5,000 raise after expecting $10,000 feels worse than a $3,000 raise after expecting nothing. This sensitivity to framing is invisible in standard utility-of-wealth models.

It also explains why money illusion is real — nominal wage cuts feel worse than real wage cuts achieved through inflation, even when economically equivalent.

concepts.title: Loss Aversion
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous finding: losses loom larger than gains. The pain of losing $100 outweighs the pleasure of gaining $100, by a factor of about 2:1 in most studies.

This explains a wide range of phenomena: the equity premium puzzle (stocks pay higher returns than bonds because investors need extra compensation for short-term losses), endowment effects (people demand more to give up an item than they'd pay to acquire it), and status quo bias (the costs of change feel worse than equivalent benefits).

Loss aversion has profound policy implications. Frame a tax cut as a loss avoided rather than a gain received. Default people into retirement plans rather than asking them to opt in — opting out feels like a loss.

concepts.title: The S-Shaped Value Function
concepts.contentHtml:
Prospect theory's value function is S-shaped: concave in gains (diminishing marginal value), convex in losses (diminishing marginal pain), and steeper for losses than gains (loss aversion).

Concave gains explain risk aversion when choosing between sure gains. The first $1,000 win matters more than the next $1,000.

Convex losses explain risk-seeking in losses. After losing $1,000, the next $1,000 hurts less, so you'll gamble to try to break even. Hence the gambler's chase.

Together, they produce the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes: risk-averse for likely gains, risk-seeking for unlikely gains (lottery tickets), risk-seeking for likely losses, risk-averse for unlikely losses (insurance).

concepts.title: Probability Weighting
concepts.contentHtml:
The second key change in prospect theory: people don't use objective probabilities. They use weighted probabilities that overweight small probabilities and underweight large ones.

This explains why people simultaneously buy lottery tickets (overweighting tiny chance of huge win) and insurance against rare disasters (overweighting tiny chance of large loss). Both involve overestimating small probabilities — the same psychological tendency.

Tversky and Kahneman's cumulative prospect theory (1992) refined the original model with rank-dependent probability weighting. The weighting function w(p) is concave for small p and convex near p = 1.

Combined, S-shaped value and inverted-S probability weighting produce the empirical patterns of choice under risk that EU theory misses — making prospect theory the dominant descriptive model of choice under uncertainty.

title: Heuristics & Biases
description: Anchoring, availability, representativeness — predictable mistakes in judgment

concepts.title: Heuristics: Useful Shortcuts
concepts.contentHtml:
A heuristic is a mental shortcut for making judgments under uncertainty. Heuristics are usually adaptive — they produce roughly correct answers fast and cheap.

The Tversky-Kahneman insight wasn't that heuristics are bad. It's that they fail in predictable ways. The same shortcut that quickly estimates a stranger's age from their appearance also produces stereotyping. The same heuristic that estimates likelihood from how easily examples come to mind also produces biased fear of plane crashes vs car crashes.

Studying heuristics means cataloguing both their successes and their systematic failures — the biases.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.contentHtml:
Anchoring: estimates are biased toward whatever number was on the table first, even when the anchor is arbitrary.

Tversky and Kahneman's classic experiment: participants spun a wheel that landed on either 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the UN. The 10-anchor group averaged 25%; the 65-anchor group averaged 45%. The wheel was clearly random — and yet it influenced answers.

Anchoring shapes negotiations (the first offer matters), pricing (a $999 'original price' anchors what counts as a deal), and forecasts (last year's number anchors next year's prediction).

The mechanism: when uncertain, we adjust from the anchor, but typically not enough. The anchor pulls our estimate toward it.

concepts.title: Availability
concepts.contentHtml:
Availability heuristic: judgments of frequency or likelihood are based on how easily examples come to mind.

Easily-recalled events seem more common. After a plane crash dominates the news, people overestimate flight risk. After a dramatic shark attack, beach attendance drops. The recent and vivid feel more likely than the distant and abstract.

Real frequencies don't always track ease of recall. Heart disease kills more Americans than car accidents, terrorism, and homicide combined — but the latter loom larger in public perception because they're more newsworthy. Availability bias has policy consequences: regulation often targets vivid hazards over statistically larger ones.

concepts.title: Representativeness & The Conjunction Fallacy
concepts.contentHtml:
Representativeness heuristic: we judge the probability of A given B by how much A resembles B.

This often serves us well — characteristic features really do correlate with category membership. But it ignores base rates and produces classic errors.

The Linda problem: 'Linda is 31, single, outspoken, and concerned with social issues.' Asked which is more probable, that Linda is (a) a bank teller, or (b) a bank teller and active in the feminist movement — most people pick (b). But (b) is a subset of (a) and must be less probable. The conjunction fallacy.

Representativeness drives stereotyping, neglect of base rates in medical testing, and the gambler's fallacy ('after five reds, black is due'). It often beats statistical reasoning in fast judgment.

concepts.title: Confirmation Bias and Overconfidence
concepts.contentHtml:
Two cognitive biases that combine to produce especially robust errors.

Confirmation bias: we seek and weight information that supports our existing beliefs. Counter-evidence gets dismissed or scrutinized; confirming evidence gets accepted easily. This makes beliefs harder to update than Bayesian rationality predicts.

Overconfidence: people are more confident in their judgments than is warranted. Surveys consistently find that 80–90% of drivers think they're above-average. Forecasters are too sure of their predictions; investors too confident of their stock picks.

Confirmation bias and overconfidence reinforce each other. We're sure we're right, we look mostly for evidence that we're right, we find it, we get even more sure.

The combined consequence: corrections are slow and painful. Real beliefs update less than perfect Bayesian agents would, especially when the question is identity-relevant or politically charged.

title: Time Inconsistency
description: Hyperbolic discounting, present bias, commitment devices

concepts.title: Standard Discounting
concepts.contentHtml:
Standard intertemporal choice uses exponential discounting: future utility is discounted by δ^t per period.

The defining property: the discount rate between any two adjacent periods is the same. Whether you're choosing between today and tomorrow, or year 30 and year 31, you weight the later period by the same factor δ.

Exponential discounting implies time consistency: a plan made today, evaluating future tradeoffs, will still be optimal tomorrow when reevaluated. No conflict between yesterday's self and today's self.

concepts.title: Hyperbolic Discounting
concepts.contentHtml:
Real preferences don't look exponential. People's discount rates are much higher for near-term tradeoffs than long-term ones.

Asked: 'Would you rather have $50 today or $100 in a year?' — many take the $50.

Asked: 'Would you rather have $50 in 5 years or $100 in 6 years?' — almost everyone takes the $100.

Same one-year delay, same payoff structure. But proximity matters. The discount rate for now-vs-soon is high; for far-vs-farther it's low.

The quasi-hyperbolic (β-δ) model captures this: U = u_0 + β·Σ δ^k·u_k. The β < 1 introduces a one-time hit on all future periods — a 'present bias.' Beyond that, normal discounting takes over.

concepts.title: Time Inconsistency
concepts.contentHtml:
Hyperbolic discounting causes a fundamental problem: preferences change over time as the choice approaches.

Today (Sunday), thinking about Monday morning, you decide to wake up early and exercise. Future-discounted, the small pain of early-rising is outweighed by the long-term health benefit.

Monday at 6 a.m., the situation has changed. The pain of waking is now now, while the benefit is still future-discounted. Present-self disagrees with Sunday-self and goes back to sleep.

Sunday-self and Monday-self have systematically different preferences — not because new information arrived, but because the time perspective shifted. This is time inconsistency: the very thing that exponential discounting precludes, hyperbolic discounting produces.

concepts.title: Sophisticated vs Naive Agents
concepts.contentHtml:
How do people respond to their own time inconsistency?

Naive agents don't realize they have a problem. They make plans assuming future-self will execute them, are repeatedly disappointed, and never adjust. Permanent New Year's resolutions.

Sophisticated agents recognize the inconsistency. They know future-self will rebel, and act now to constrain future-self.

Sophisticated agents seek commitment devices: actions taken now that bind future choices. Christmas savings accounts (which charge fees for early withdrawal). Ulysses tying himself to the mast. Apps that lock you out of social media. Throwing out the cigarettes.

The best commitment devices have the property that you'll thank yourself later — by removing the option to behave badly when temptation arrives, you secure the better outcome both selves agree on at calm moments.

concepts.title: Policy Implications
concepts.contentHtml:
Time inconsistency reframes a wide range of policy issues.

Retirement saving: people consistently undersave because future-self prefers more saving than present-self does. Auto-enrollment, employer match, and Save More Tomorrow programs (Thaler-Benartzi) reduce undersaving without restricting choice.

Health behaviors: smoking, drinking, sedentary lifestyles all reflect present-bias. Sin taxes, sugar bans, and 'commit to quit' programs target the gap between long-run and short-run preferences.

Procrastination: O'Donoghue and Rabin showed how present-bias produces persistent task-postponement. Deadlines, penalties, and external accountability are commitment devices.

The libertarian-paternalist position (Sunstein-Thaler) holds that present-bias is real, well-documented, and that policy can use this to help people pursue their own stated goals — without forcing them to. This is the foundation of nudge theory.

title: Nudges & Choice Architecture
description: Defaults, framing, libertarian paternalism — Thaler and Sunstein

concepts.title: Choice Architecture
concepts.contentHtml:
Every decision is presented in some way — there's no neutral framing. The arrangement of options, default choice, ordering, and visual presentation all influence what's chosen. Choice architecture is the deliberate design of this presentation.

Sunstein-Thaler's central observation: choice architecture is unavoidable, so we might as well design it thoughtfully rather than by accident. Cafeterias must arrange food in some order; forms must have some default; menus must list items somehow.

The shift in mindset: from 'just give people more information and they'll choose well' to 'recognize how the presentation itself shapes choice and design accordingly.'

concepts.title: Defaults
concepts.contentHtml:
The most powerful nudge is the default option — what happens if you do nothing.

Organ donation: countries with opt-in systems have ~15% participation; opt-out countries have ~90%, despite identical underlying preferences. The difference is simply who has to take action.

Retirement saving: switching 401(k) plans from opt-in to opt-out raises participation from around 40% to over 90%. Madrian and Shea (2001) documented this dramatic effect.

Why defaults dominate: status quo bias, present bias (action takes effort now, benefits are deferred), and the implicit signal — 'this is what most people choose / what experts recommend.'

Defaults are extraordinarily cheap and effective policy levers. They preserve the freedom to opt out while shifting average behavior substantially.

concepts.title: Framing Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
The same option, described differently, elicits different choices. Framing matters.

Surgery survival: '90% survive' vs '10% die.' Same fact, different acceptance rates.

Discount vs surcharge: a $1 'cash discount' or '$1 credit-card surcharge' — same prices, but credit-card use is much higher under the discount frame.

Goal framing: '$1 off after taxes' or '4% saving' — math equivalent, different appeal.

Loss aversion underlies many framing effects. Whatever can be presented as a loss avoided generally outperforms the same thing presented as a gain achieved. Public-health messaging that frames inaction as a loss tends to outperform messages that frame action as a gain.

concepts.title: Libertarian Paternalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Sunstein and Thaler's term for policy that nudges without forcing. Libertarian: people retain full freedom to choose. Paternalistic: the design isn't neutral; it's aimed at helping people pursue their own stated goals.

The argument for the position: choice architecture is unavoidable, so neutrality is a fiction. Bad architecture imposes harm; good architecture helps people. Both leave choice intact.

The argument against: who decides what's 'good for' people? Defaults can be misused, manipulated, or capture-prone. The line between nudge and manipulation isn't always clear.

The framework has been controversial but enormously influential. The UK's Behavioural Insights Team (the 'Nudge Unit') was founded on it, and most OECD governments now have similar units. Sunstein wrote much of the policy framework into US regulation during the Obama administration.

concepts.title: When Nudges Work — and When They Don't
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2010s nudge boom produced a wave of small, robust effects on simple choices: opt-out organ donation, retirement auto-enrollment, simplified financial disclosures, calorie labels, default privacy settings.

The 2020s wave of meta-analyses produced more sober estimates. Many flashy individual results don't replicate. Effects are often smaller than originally claimed (Mertens et al. found ~1.4% behavior change averaged across nudges, smaller than initial claims). And nudges work less well on big, motivated decisions and on already-engaged populations.

The honest current view: nudges are real, useful, and cheap, but not a panacea. They complement — don't replace — traditional policy tools (price signals, regulation, public investment). And the design has to be careful: poorly-aimed nudges can mislead, manipulate, or simply fail to budge entrenched habits.

The deeper insight survives: choice architecture isn't optional. The question isn't whether to nudge but how to design the architecture you can't avoid having.
